newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - W. Digital to raise Asia output.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - W. Digital to raise Asia output.

text.p: Western Digital Corp (WD) plans to spend up to US$100 million to double the disk drive output of its Singapore and Malaysia plants, WD's president, chairman and chief executive officer said.
WD President Charles Haggerty told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday that fresh investments in the two countries would be "probably in the order of about $75 million to $100 million."

Haggerty said Wall Street analysts are estimating WD's production for the financial year ending June 1997 at 20-21 million units "and I am comfortable with that." The company produced 15.5 million disk drives for the year to June 1996.
On Wednesday, WD opened in Tuas in Singapore its first plant in the world to manufacture high-end hard disk enterprise drives designed for workstations and local area network (LAN) servers.

"By the year 2000, we would have invested $35 million here in Tuas. We will have invested $220 million in the Chai Chee plant (in Singapore) and another $150 million in the Malaysian plant," Haggerty said at the site of the new plant.
The new Tuas plant has already produced 250,000 units since it began operations in April and is expected to commence volume shipment in 30 days.
Capacity would be raised from the current 250,000 units per quarter to 750,000 by year 2000, Haggerty said.
WD will be dedicating the opening of a second disk drive production facility for personal storage in Malaysia on Thursday.
Following the startup of the second facility in Malaysia, the plant's share of total output within the company would rise to 50 percent.
Output at the company's Chai Chee facility in Singapore, which also produces disk drives exclusively for the personal storage group, would also double by the end of 1998.
Haggerty said disk drive demand is strong for 1996 and the company is almost sold out for this quarter.
"We have a number of products on allocation. Most of our products are on allocation," he said.
Turning to the company's new Enterprise Storage Group, Haggerty said that it would grow signifanctly and "by 1999...that would be as much as a billion dollar business".
He expected the new group to contribute between 10 and 15 percent to total revenue by the year 2000.
The company formed the new Enterprise Storage Group in late 1994 to expand its data storage business into the enterprise computing business.
Analysts are predicting that WD's revenue in fiscal 1997 would be between $3.9 billion to $4 billion, up from $2.86 billion for the previous financial year, Haggerty said.
